findings.location: src/haute/_code_extraction.py:919-981 (extract_user_code) + 700-735 (_finalise_polars) + 146-182 (_rewrite_outer_returns_as_assignment) + 185-226 (_strip_outer_trailing_return) + 335-386 (_strip_generated_passthrough_from_code); driven by src/haute/_config_builder.py:74-233 (_build_node_config) which calls one _extract_*_user_code per node on the healthy parse path (src/haute/parser.py:144,153-154)
findings.title: Each node body is re-parsed with ast.parse 3-4 times per GUI load, discarding the module AST that was already built once
findings.description: The healthy parser parses the whole file exactly once (parser.py:144 `tree = ast.parse(source)`) and _extract_function_bodies (parser.py:153) walks that tree to slice each function body out as TEXT. That body text is then handed to _build_node_config -> extract_user_code, which throws away the already-parsed AST subtree and re-runs ast.parse on the same body several times. For the common polars/transform path the body is parsed: (1) in _strip_trailing_return -> _strip_outer_trailing_return -> _outermost_returns -> _parse_user_code; then inside _finalise_polars: (2) _strip_generated_passthrough_from_code -> _is_exact_passthrough_return -> _parse_user_code (unconditional when params present), (3) _df_alias_target -> ast.parse(lines[0]) (unconditional), and (4) _rewrite_outer_returns_as_assignment -> _outermost_returns -> _parse_user_code. _unwrap_chain_assignment adds up to 2 more ast.parse calls for `df = (...)` bodies. modelScore/ratingStep add further _rewrite_identifier_tokens -> _parse_user_code passes. Nothing is memoised; the same source string is tokenised and parsed into a fresh ast.Module 3-6x per node. This is pure repeated work: every parse rebuilds the identical tree.
findings.evidence: Per-node parse count for a typical transform body (non-passthrough, not starting with `df = (`): _outermost_returns(parse #1, via _strip_trailing_return at line 974) + _is_exact_passthrough_return(parse #2, line 339) + _df_alias_target(parse #3, line 350) + _rewrite_outer_returns_as_assignment->_outermost_returns(parse #4, line 734). All four operate on the SAME body text. ast.parse is the dominant cost in each helper (tokeniser + parser allocate a full node tree). The information each helper needs (top-level Return nodes, first-statement shape, df-alias) is all derivable from ONE parse of the body, and in fact from the function subtree already present in the module `tree` that parser.py:144 produced.
findings.when_it_bites: Every GUI load / preview / save-reload of a healthy pipeline (parse_pipeline_file runs on each). Cost scales linearly with node count but with a 3-6x constant on the per-node ast.parse. Bites hardest on large ratebooks with many code-bearing nodes (transform/ratingStep/modelScore/scenarioExpander), each carrying a non-trivial body (tens of lines of Polars). At ~100-300 such nodes the redundant parses turn a single-digit-ms parse into tens of ms of avoidable CPU on the interactive load path; on very large pipelines (500+ nodes) it is the difference between a snappy and a visibly laggy canvas open.
findings.recommended_fix: Parse each node body at most once and thread the resulting ast.Module (or, better, reuse the FunctionDef subtree already available in the module `tree` from parser.py:144 rather than re-slicing text and re-parsing at all). Concretely: change _outermost_returns / _is_exact_passthrough_return / _df_alias_target / _rewrite_outer_returns_as_assignment / _strip_redundant_rhs_wrapper_once to accept a pre-parsed tree, and have extract_user_code parse the (dedented) body a single time, passing that tree to every consumer. The textual line/col rewriting can still run off the one tree. This removes 2-5 ast.parse calls per node with no behavioural change.

findings.title: Regex-fallback connect recovery rescans the whole source from index 0 once (often twice) per connect anchor → O(edges x source_length)
findings.description: For every `pipeline.connect(` anchor the fallback does multiple scans that each start at index 0 and run up to the anchor offset, making the pass O(A * n) where A = number of connect anchors (≈ number of edges) and n = source length. Specifically, _iter_connect_anchor_matches already calls _is_top_level_statement_anchor(source, m.start()) (line 270), which calls _parenthesized_wrapper_depth_before(source, idx) — a full character walk `while i < idx` from 0 (lines 116-139). Then _find_connect_calls, for the SAME anchor, computes the line number with source.count('\n', 0, m.start()) (line 337, scan 0->start) and calls _parenthesized_wrapper_depth_before(source, m.start()) AGAIN (line 338) — recomputing byte-for-byte the wrapper depth that _is_top_level_statement_anchor already computed for that exact index. So each anchor triggers ~3 left-to-right scans of the prefix, two of which are identical string-aware walks. Because connect calls in a generated ratebook scale with edges, and edges scale with nodes, and n scales with nodes, the real growth is roughly O(nodes^2).
findings.evidence: _parenthesized_wrapper_depth_before walks every prefix char with string/comment skipping (lines 116-139: `while i < idx: _skip_string_literal(...); ...`). It is invoked once per anchor inside _is_top_level_statement_anchor (line 180, reached from _iter_connect_anchor_matches:270) and a SECOND time on the same index in _find_connect_calls:338. Plus source.count('\n', 0, m.start()) at line 337 is a third 0->start scan. Net: ~3 * sum(anchor_offsets) char visits ≈ O(A*n), with the line-338 scan being provably redundant with the line-180 scan (same source, same index, deterministic result).
findings.when_it_bites: Only on the syntax-error fallback path (parser.py:145-147 triggers it solely when ast.parse raises). It bites when a user has a broken-but-large generated/ratebook file open in the editor — exactly when they are mid-edit and the canvas re-parses on every keystroke-debounce. A 2,000-line file with ~200 connect() calls performs on the order of 200 * (avg 1,000-char prefix) * 3 ≈ 600k extra char visits per parse, repeated on every edit while the file stays broken. For 5,000-line files with 500 edges this is multi-million-char-visit per parse and becomes perceptible interactive lag precisely while the user is trying to fix the error.
findings.recommended_fix: Two independent wins: (1) Eliminate the duplicate scan — have _iter_connect_anchor_matches yield (match, wrapper_depth) so _find_connect_calls reuses the wrapper depth instead of recomputing it at line 338. (2) Replace the repeated source.count('\n', 0, idx) line-number lookups with a single precomputed prefix newline-offset array (bisect over line-start offsets) so line numbers are O(log n) instead of O(n) each. Both keep behaviour identical and drop the connect pass from ~O(A*n) toward O(n + A log n).

findings.title: Fallback decorator/function discovery re-scans source from index 0 per decorator anchor via _position_is_code (O(decorators x source_length))
findings.description: _find_function_blocks iterates every `@pipeline.<type>` anchor from _RE_DECORATOR_ANCHOR.finditer and, for each, calls _position_is_code(source, m.start()) (line 517). _position_is_code walks from index 0 to the anchor with full string/comment skipping (lines 363-377: `i = 0; while i < idx`). With D decorator anchors this is O(D * n). On top of that, the per-block helpers compute line numbers with source.count('\n', 0, idx) at multiple sites (_recover_decorator_text:436, _find_decorated_def:498, and the connect/meta recovery), each an additional 0->idx scan. _recover_pipeline_meta:389 also calls _position_is_code per meta anchor. The same prefix is therefore walked once per decorator just to answer the boolean 'is this anchor inside a string/comment'.
findings.evidence: _position_is_code is a from-zero scan (line 363 `i = 0`). It is called once per decorator anchor in _find_function_blocks:517 and once per meta anchor in _recover_pipeline_meta:389. For D decorators at average offset n/2, total work ≈ D*n/2 char visits, on top of the connect-path scans (separate finding). Line-number computations via source.count('\n', 0, idx) recur at decorator/def/connect/meta sites, none sharing a precomputed index.
findings.when_it_bites: Fallback-only (broken file). Decorator count D equals node count, so on a broken large ratebook (e.g. 300 @pipeline nodes in a 3,000-line file) this is ~300 * ~1,500-char prefix ≈ 450k char visits per parse purely for the in-code checks, compounding with the connect-path quadratic on every re-parse while the file is broken. Negligible for small files; only material at large-pipeline scale during error-state editing.
findings.recommended_fix: Compute string/comment 'code regions' for the source ONCE (a single left-to-right pass producing a sorted list of (start,end) code spans, reusing _skip_string_literal), then make _position_is_code a bisect membership test (O(log n)) instead of a from-zero walk. Share the same precomputed newline-offset array used by the connect fix for all source.count('\n', 0, idx) line-number lookups. This makes decorator discovery O(n + D log n) with identical results.

findings.title: evaluate_expression re-parses the same code 2-3x per call and discards the AST + located target node it already computed
findings.description: A single evaluate_expression(code, col, ...) runs ast.parse on the identical code string 2 times for a plain column and 3 times for a conditional column, and each parse is followed by a fresh _build_safe_symbol_table, _resolve_reassignment_chains, _find_with_columns_calls, and _extract_expressions_from_with_columns over the WHOLE module. _parse_expression_impl already parses the tree, builds the symbol table, and locates the exact target best_match node; then _compute_result_impl throws all of that away and re-parses + re-builds + re-locates the same node, and for conditionals _evaluate_conditional_branches does it a THIRD time. The parsed tree, symbol table, and target node are pure functions of (code, target_column) yet nothing is shared or memoised.
findings.evidence: Instrumented the unmodified module (wrapped ast.parse + walk helpers) via .venv python. Per single call: CONDITIONAL column = {ast.parse:3, find_with_columns:3, build_symbol_table:3, resolve_reassignment_chains:3}; ARITHMETIC column = {ast.parse:2, find_wc:2, build_sym:2, resolve_chains:2}. Wall time (2000-iter timeit, 2-col node): conditional 367 us/call, arithmetic 247 us/call, vs parse_expression ALONE 117 us/call -- ~2-3x of the cost is pure re-parse overhead. _compute_result_impl:1549-1567 re-runs the same ast.parse + symbol-table + wc-extraction that _parse_expression_impl:1021-1086 already ran.
findings.when_it_bites: Every traced cell, for every step that created/passed the clicked column, for every element of the intra-node dependency chain. The 2-3x constant sits on top of the chain/step amplification. Worst on conditional pl.when/then/otherwise columns (the rating-logic columns actuaries trace most) which pay the 3x path.
findings.recommended_fix: Parse once per (code, target_column): have _parse_expression_impl return/cache the parsed tree, symbol_table, and located target node and pass them into _compute_result / _evaluate_conditional_branches instead of re-deriving. A functools.lru_cache keyed on the code string for the heavy invariant part (tree, symbol_table, wc_calls) is the lowest-risk behavior-preserving change and also fixes finding 2; node code strings are small/bounded. (review/03-simplification rejected the textual dedup of the four loops for bundling a behavior change -- caching the deterministic parse is different and is the real win.)

findings.title: Chain enrichment is O(N^2) in node width x chain depth: parse_expression_chain re-parses per chain element, then enrich_steps re-evaluates per chain element, each a full whole-node re-parse
findings.description: parse_expression_chain does its own ast.parse + symbol-table + _find_with_columns_calls, builds a converter for EVERY column in the node (2186-2196), then for each column in the dependency chain calls parse_expression(code_wrapped, col) AGAIN (line 2227), each re-parsing the whole node. enrich_steps then loops over that chain (1559-1568) calling evaluate_expression(raw_code, p.target_column, ...) per element, each of which triggers the 2-3 internal re-parses from finding 1. For a chain of length K from a with_columns block of width N, one traced cell pays O(K) outer iterations x O(N) per-parse extraction x the 2-3x internal factor ~ O(N*K) ast.parse passes and O(N*K*N) total walk/extract work. When K~N (each-column-derives-from-previous rating ladder) this is quadratic-to-cubic in node width.
findings.evidence: Measured exact enrich_steps per-column work (parse_expression + evaluate_expression + parse_expression_chain + evaluate_expression-per-chain-element) on a single with_columns node of width N with a full-depth chain, unmodified module, .venv python: N=5 -> 19 ast.parse calls, 2.68 ms for ONE traced cell; N=20 -> 64 ast.parse, 36.6 ms; N=50 -> 154 ast.parse, 190.3 ms. Wall time grows ~N^1.9 confirming quadratic total work though raw parse COUNT is ~3N+4. 154 ast.parse calls to explain one clicked cell on a 50-wide node is the headline.
findings.when_it_bites: Tracing a cell in a wide rating/banding node (one with_columns producing many derived columns where each builds on the last -- extremely common in insurance ratebooks). At ~50 derived columns one cell costs ~190 ms pure CPU in the parser; at ~100 columns ~0.7-1 s/cell. enrich_steps also walks every step, so a deep graph with several such nodes multiplies further. Trace/preview feels janky exactly on the large ratebooks the engine targets.
findings.recommended_fix: (1) Parse the node ONCE and reuse tree+symbol_table+wc_calls for all chain elements instead of calling parse_expression per element at 2227 (build each ParsedExpression from the col_defs already computed at 2199-2201). (2) In enrich_steps, since the chain is already parsed, expose a single chain-evaluate entry so the per-element evaluate_expression at 1563 does not re-parse -- or apply the lru_cache from finding 1, collapsing all duplicate ast.parse to one per distinct code string. Either fix removes the N factor; together a cell becomes O(N).

findings.title: Every parse pass re-walks the whole module and re-extracts/re-converts ALL columns to find ONE target, with no early-out
findings.description: _find_with_columns_calls does a full ast.walk(tree) of the entire module on every invocation. _parse_expression_impl additionally walks three more times (_has_control_flow_wrapping_target, _find_control_flow_assigned_vars, _build_safe_symbol_table) before it looks for the target. The last-match-wins search (1081-1086, mirrored at _compute_result_impl 1562-1566 and _evaluate_conditional_branches 1466-1471) calls _extract_expressions_from_with_columns for EVERY with_columns call, and parse_expression_chain builds a full _ExprConverter for EVERY column -- though only one target_column is wanted. No short-circuit on alias match, no reuse of walk results across passes within one parse. This O(node-width) factor is what findings 1 and 2 multiply against.
findings.evidence: Code trace: _find_with_columns_calls:917 for node in ast.walk(tree) (whole module). _parse_expression_impl:1044/1058/1055 invoke the two control-flow walkers (each ast.walk per top-level cf stmt, 854-863/878-891) + _build_safe_symbol_table. Search at 1081-1086 iterates all wc_calls x all exprs with no break on match. parse_expression_chain:2186-2196 builds _ExprConverter(...).convert(expr_node) for every (expr_node, alias) regardless of target. Instrumentation showed find_with_columns runs 2-3x PER evaluate_expression, each a full-module walk.
findings.when_it_bites: Scales with number of with_columns/statements in the blob and columns per block. The executor usually wraps one node's code, so wide nodes make each walk + extraction O(width); combined with per-call and per-chain-element re-parsing, this is the inner multiplier turning a 50-column node into 190 ms/cell. On its own (single parse_expression) it is a modest constant and only matters through the multiplication -- fix together with the caching above, not in isolation.
findings.recommended_fix: Short-circuit the target search (scan wc_calls in reverse, take first alias hit to preserve documented last-match-wins B005 semantics -- verify against that test before reordering). Build per-column converters in parse_expression_chain only for chain members. Most importantly cache _find_with_columns_calls + the symbol table on the parsed tree so the 2-3 passes within one evaluate_expression share a single walk. Bounded by small node blobs, so the absolute win is meaningful only at large node width; prioritise behind findings 1 and 2.

findings.title: Operator dispatch dicts rebuilt on every binop/compare evaluation (minor -- NOT worth fixing alone)
findings.description: _binop constructs a fresh 9-entry op_map mapping ast types to operator functions on every call, and _compare builds a 6-entry cmp_map on every comparison. These are module-constant tables (the module already hoists _OP_SYMBOLS/_CMP_SYMBOLS/_PREC at top level) but here are re-allocated per AST node during evaluation. Easy to flag but negligible vs the ast.parse cost dominating this module.
findings.evidence: Lines 1621-1631 define op_map = {ast.Add: operator.add, ...} inside _binop; 1657-1664 define cmp_map = {...} inside _compare, recreated per evaluated node. Measured impact is in the noise: evaluation is a tiny fraction of the 117-367 us/call dominated by parsing + symbol-table building, so eliminating these saves well under 1% of a trace cell.
findings.when_it_bites: Only at extreme expression-tree node counts during evaluation, which never dominates because per-call parse cost is 100-300x larger. Included for calibration: a premature micro-optimisation in isolation -- do NOT spend a dev/reviewer pair on it. If touched, hoist in the same diff as findings 1-3; otherwise leave it.
findings.recommended_fix: Hoist op_map and cmp_map to module-level frozen dicts (mirroring _OP_SYMBOLS/_CMP_SYMBOLS at 61-87) and reference them; zero behavior change. Bundle opportunistically with the real fixes.

results.coverage_note: Read src/haute/executor.py (1600 lines) and src/haute/_execute_lazy.py (2048 lines) in full, plus the cost-center functions they call: graph_fingerprint / canonical_json / _canonicalise / preamble_execution_fingerprint / GraphFingerprintMemo (_cache.py), runtime_input_extra_keys / _runtime_file_inputs_signature / _stat_gated_runtime_path_fingerprint / canonical_dataframe_execution_graph (execution.py), cache_state_signature_for_graph (_json_flatten.py), prepare_graph (projection.py), and PipelineGraph cached properties (_types.py). Cross-checked review/00-map/architecture.md perf section (which rates these files 'well-engineered', medium priority) and review/03-simplification/complexity-metrics.md, and verified none of these perf items appear in review/02-findings or review/04-exhaustive (those are correctness/concurrency findings on the same lines). The code IS largely well-optimised on the genuine hot paths: the structural graph fingerprint is per-instance @cached_property memoised; preamble compile is lru_cache(128) with a force_refresh=False fast path for sink/optimiser loops; runtime-file fingerprints are stat-gated (one stat() per file, content re-hash only on metadata change); per-node collect_schema() results are cached in column_cache keyed by (node_id, port); fully-opaque contracts short-circuit via _should_check_contract; checkpoint projection pushdown and .cache() on diamond fan-outs are present. Findings below are the residual repeated-per-request work, ordered by realistic impact. I did not execute or profile (read-only audit); impact estimates are from code-path cost reasoning, not measured numbers.

findings.location: src/haute/executor.py:901-909 (execute_graph extra_keys + graph_fingerprint, runs unconditionally before the cache lookup)
findings.title: Per-preview cache-key build re-serialises and re-hashes runtime-input signatures via canonical_json on every click, including pure cache hits
findings.description: execute_graph computes extra_keys = [..., *runtime_input_extra_keys(graph)] and then fp = graph_fingerprint(graph, *extra_keys) BEFORE the _preview_cache.try_get(fp) lookup, so this work runs on every request including the common case where the user clicks a different node on an unchanged graph (a guaranteed cache hit). runtime_input_extra_keys -> _runtime_file_inputs_signature rebuilds a per-file-node entries list and calls content_hash_bytes(canonical_json(entries).encode()); _canonicalise recurses the whole entries structure and json.dumps(sort_keys=True) re-serialises it every call. cache_state_signature_for_graph similarly walks every apiInput node and stats two sidecar meta.json files per node. The stat-gating (one stat() per data file) correctly avoids re-hashing file BYTES, but the canonical_json serialisation + content hash of the assembled signature, and the apiInput sidecar double-stat, are redone from scratch each preview even when the inputs are byte-identical to the previous click.
findings.evidence: Cost per preview click is O(file_input_nodes) stats + one canonical_json+blake over the entries list, plus O(apiInput_nodes)*2 sidecar stats + _path_hash. For a graph with N file-backed dataSources and M apiInputs this is N+2M stat() syscalls + a JSON re-encode of an N-element nested mapping, on every click, even on a 100% cache hit. graph_fingerprint then does another content_hash_bytes over the joined extra_keys+base string. None of this is memoised across calls on the same (unchanged) graph instance the way _haute_base_fingerprint is.
findings.when_it_bites: Frequent previews on graphs with many file-backed inputs or many apiInput nodes (e.g. a 30-source ratebook pipeline the user is clicking through node-by-node). At ~50 file/apiInput nodes that is ~50-100 stat() syscalls + a JSON re-encode per click; on networked/Windows filesystems stat latency dominates and makes every otherwise-instant cache hit cost milliseconds of syscall time. Negligible for small graphs (<5 inputs).
findings.recommended_fix: Memoise the runtime-input signature on the PipelineGraph instance behind the same stat-gate the file fingerprints already use: cache (signature_string, per-file stat_gate tuple) on the graph and recompute only the entries whose (mtime_ns,size) sidecar/stat changed, rather than re-serialising the whole entries list. Equivalently, hoist runtime_input_extra_keys into a request-scoped memo keyed by graph identity + the cheap stat tuples so repeated clicks on the same unchanged graph reuse the assembled key. The stat() calls themselves are the irreducible freshness floor; the canonical_json re-encode and blake over unchanged entries are not.

findings.location: src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:120-122 and 704 (_resolve_graph_paths in _execute_lazy) + 1605 (_resolve_graph_paths in _execute_eager_core) -> execution.py:163-193 canonical_dataframe_execution_graph
findings.title: canonical_dataframe_execution_graph re-walks and re-resolves every node's file path on each eager/lazy execute, unmemoised
findings.description: Both _execute_eager_core (line 1605) and _execute_lazy (line 704) call _resolve_graph_paths(graph) = canonical_dataframe_execution_graph(graph) as their first step. That function iterates all graph.nodes, calls _graph_runtime_path_config_key(node) per node, and for file-bearing nodes calls resolve_runtime_file_path (filesystem path resolution). It returns the same graph unchanged when no path differs, but it still pays the full O(nodes) walk + per-file-node path resolution every call. On the preview path this runs once per cache miss/extend; on optimiser/training loops that call execute_lazy repeatedly on the same graph it runs every iteration. The result is also a fresh model_copy when any path changed, which discards the per-instance _haute_base_fingerprint cache on the copy (though the fingerprint used by execute_graph is computed on the original instance, so that particular cache is preserved upstream).
findings.evidence: canonical_dataframe_execution_graph (execution.py:168-193): `for node in graph.nodes: ... resolve_runtime_file_path(raw_path, source_file=..., prefer='project')`. resolve_runtime_file_path does Path resolution (and potentially project-root walking) per file node. No @cached_property or instance memo guards it, unlike node_map/parents_of/_haute_base_fingerprint which are memoised. Called at _execute_lazy.py:704 and _execute_lazy.py:1605.
findings.when_it_bites: Optimiser ratebook solves and training jobs that call _execute_lazy in a tight loop over the SAME graph (path resolution result is invariant across iterations) — the per-iteration node walk + path .resolve() is pure waste there. For interactive preview it is a single walk per cache miss, so low impact. Scales with node count and number of file-backed nodes.
findings.recommended_fix: Memoise the canonicalised graph on the PipelineGraph instance (a @cached_property or a module-level WeakKeyDictionary keyed by graph identity), invalidated by model_copy the same way _haute_base_fingerprint is. Since path resolution depends only on (node configs, source_file) — all immutable on a given instance — the resolved graph can be computed once per instance and reused by every execute call.

findings.location: src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:180-227 (_effective_contract) called at 1120 (_build_lazy_node) and 1767 (_execute_eager_core), per node per execute
findings.title: _effective_contract is rebuilt per node on every execute (and separately on eager and lazy paths) instead of being cached per (nodeType, config)
findings.description: When enforce_contracts is True (the production default), every node calls contract = _effective_contract(node) once per execution. _effective_contract calls Contract.from_tuple(get_column_contract(node.data.nodeType, node.data.config)) — which for rating/banding/modelScore nodes parses the node's config (tables, factors, columns) to derive the read/produce column sets — then overlays the user-declared contract via projection_planner.overlay_declared_contract. This derivation is a pure function of (nodeType, config) and the config is immutable for a given graph instance, yet it is recomputed: (a) once per node every preview cache miss/extend, and (b) again, independently, on the lazy path for sink/deploy. The column_cache in both functions caches the RESULT of collect_schema() but not the contract derivation itself.
findings.evidence: _execute_eager_core line 1767: `contract = _effective_contract(node) if enforce_contracts else None` inside `for nid in order:`. _build_lazy_node line 1120: identical call inside the per-node build. get_column_contract for a rating node walks config['tables'][*]['factors'] / ['entries']; for banding walks config['factors']; this O(config size) parse happens per node per execute. Two separate call sites (eager + lazy) means a graph previewed then sunk derives every contract twice.
findings.when_it_bites: Large ratebooks where rating/banding nodes carry big tables/factors lists in config: get_column_contract's per-node config walk is O(table_entries) and runs for every node on every cache miss. A 50-rating-step pipeline with large factor lists pays this whole derivation on each first-click of a new target (cache miss) and on each sink. Opaque-heavy graphs (user POLARS transforms) are cheaper because _should_check_contract skips the boundary check — but _effective_contract itself still runs to DECIDE that.
findings.recommended_fix: Cache the builder-derived Contract keyed by (nodeType, canonical-config-hash) — or memoise on the GraphNode/config object — so repeated executes and the eager/lazy split reuse one derivation. overlay_declared_contract is cheap; the get_column_contract config parse is the cost. Given configs are immutable per instance, a module-level cache keyed on id(config) (or the already-available canonical_json of the config used in the base fingerprint) eliminates the repeat.

findings.location: src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:1720-1723 (_schema_items_of) invoked at 1917, 1924, plus 1932 second build for MODEL_SCORE in _execute_eager_core
findings.title: Eager core computes each node's schema via collect_schema() two-to-three times per node (available, post-rename output, and a recomputed model-score available set)
findings.description: For every materialised node, _execute_eager_core calls _schema_items_of(result_lf) at line 1917 (available_columns, pre-select), then _schema_items_of(output_lf) at line 1924 (full_output_columns, post-select/rename). Each call does lazy_frame.collect_schema() and builds a list of (name, str(dtype)) tuples. collect_schema() walks the lazy plan to resolve the schema; doing it twice per node resolves the (largely overlapping) plan twice. For MODEL_SCORE nodes without code/renames/selected_columns, available_columns[nid] is then RE-ASSIGNED to full_output_columns at line 1932 — making the line-1917 schema computation for that node entirely wasted work. The lazy path's column_cache caches frozenset column sets across the producer/consumer boundary, but this eager-core schema duplication is within a single node's own processing and is not deduplicated.
findings.evidence: Line 1917 `available_columns[nid] = _schema_items_of(result_lf)`; line 1924 `full_output_columns = _schema_items_of(output_lf)`; line 1926-1932 for MODEL_SCORE re-sets `available_columns[nid] = full_output_columns`, discarding the 1917 result. When selected_columns/renames are absent, result_lf and output_lf have the SAME schema, so the two collect_schema() calls resolve identical plans.
findings.when_it_bites: Wide frames (hundreds of columns — common after joins in a rating pipeline) where collect_schema() and the list-comprehension over schema.names() are O(columns) each, run twice per node, once per preview cache miss across all materialised ancestors. At ~30 nodes x ~300 cols this is ~9000 redundant (name,dtype) tuple builds + a duplicate plan-schema walk per cache miss. Modest in absolute terms but pure waste on the interactive miss path.
findings.recommended_fix: When _apply_selected_columns and _apply_column_renames are both no-ops (the common case — detectable cheaply from config presence), reuse the result_lf schema for output_lf instead of recomputing. For MODEL_SCORE-without-transforms, skip the line-1917 available_columns computation entirely since it is immediately overwritten. Cache the collect_schema() result once per node and derive both available/output column lists from it.

findings.location: src/haute/executor.py:1259-1306 (_eager_execute) -> _compile_preamble with force_refresh=True default, run on every preview cache miss/extend
findings.title: Preview path recomputes the preamble execution fingerprint (AST walk + utility-file hashing pipeline) on every cache miss even when the preamble is unchanged
findings.description: _eager_execute (the preview executor body) calls _compile_preamble(graph.preamble or '', pipeline_dir=..., memo=fingerprint_memo) with the default force_refresh=True. That triggers preamble_execution_fingerprint, which: (1) calls preamble_imports_utility(preamble) (an AST parse/walk of the preamble text) to decide whether utility files are relevant, and (2) when utility is imported, hashes nearby utility.py/utility/**/*.py via _hash_utility_candidate, then canonical_json-serialises the parts and content-hashes them — all to produce the lru_cache key for _compile_preamble_cached. The actual compile is lru_cache-hit when unchanged, but the FINGERPRINT computation that gates it runs in full on every preview miss. The fingerprint_memo (GraphFingerprintMemo) deduplicates utility-file hashing within a single execute_graph call but NOT across clicks. Contrast the sink path (line 1497) which correctly passes force_refresh=False to skip this entirely.
findings.evidence: executor.py:1295 `preamble_ns = _compile_preamble(graph.preamble or '', pipeline_dir=_pipeline_dir(graph), memo=fingerprint_memo)` — no force_refresh, so default True. _compile_preamble (line 438) `if force_refresh: execution_fingerprint = preamble_execution_fingerprint(...)`. preamble_execution_fingerprint re-runs preamble_imports_utility (AST parse) + canonical_json over parts every call. The GraphFingerprintMemo is created fresh per execute_graph (executor.py:865 `fingerprint_memo = GraphFingerprintMemo()`), so cross-click reuse is zero.
findings.when_it_bites: Pipelines with a non-trivial preamble that imports a utility PACKAGE (utility/**/*.py): each preview cache miss re-stats and conditionally re-hashes every utility file (stat-gated, so usually just stats) AND re-parses the preamble AST + re-serialises the parts list. For a utility package with many modules, that is one stat() per module per cache miss plus an AST parse of the preamble. Correct for freshness (GUI utility edits must invalidate), but the AST re-parse and canonical_json re-encode are recomputable-once-per-instance. Empty/utility-free preambles are unaffected (short-circuited).
findings.recommended_fix: Memoise preamble_imports_utility(preamble) and the assembled fingerprint per (preamble text, pipeline_dir) behind the stat gate — only the utility-file stat tuples need re-checking each call; the AST walk and the canonical_json of parts are pure functions of unchanged inputs. Alternatively cache the preamble_execution_fingerprint on the graph instance keyed by the utility stat tuples, recomputing only when a stat gate moves.

findings.title: Preamble-error injection rebuilds node_map with a dict comprehension instead of using the cached graph.node_map property
findings.description: In executor._eager_execute, when a PreambleError occurred, the error-injection block builds `node_map = {n.id: n for n in graph.nodes}` (executor.py:1327) to look up node types for POLARS/LIVE_SWITCH nodes. PipelineGraph already exposes graph.node_map as a memoised @cached_property (built once per instance), so this comprehension re-materialises the same dict, allocating a fresh O(nodes) dict every time a preamble fails. Minor, and only on the error path, but it is a gratuitous re-build of an already-cached structure and slightly contradicts the codebase's own per-instance memoisation discipline.
findings.evidence: executor.py:1327 `node_map = {n.id: n for n in graph.nodes}` inside `if preamble_error:`. _types.py:697-700 defines `@cached_property def node_map(self): return {n.id: n for n in self.nodes}`. The local re-build duplicates it.
findings.when_it_bites: Only when a preamble fails to compile (error path), so frequency is low; cost is one redundant O(nodes) dict allocation per failed-preamble execute. Negligible at any scale but a free cleanup that aligns with the memoisation already in place. Flagged for completeness, not urgency.
findings.recommended_fix: Use `node_map = graph.node_map` (the cached property) instead of rebuilding the dict. The eager/lazy cores receive a re-canonicalised graph, but the cached property on that instance is equally valid; if the canonicalised copy's cache is cold this still computes once and memoises for any later use.

findings.location: src/haute/chunking.py:1011-1015 (_project_frame call per node per chunk) + 1514-1535 (_project_frame body, collect_schema at 1522); compounded by 1009-1010 (_apply_selected_columns/_apply_column_renames)
findings.title: Per-chunk collect_schema() storm: chunk-invariant node schemas are re-resolved O(nodes x chunks) times in the runner loop
findings.description: Inside iter_chunked_frames the per-chunk loop (lines 975-1016) re-derives every chunk node's output schema on every chunk. For each non-start chunk node, _project_frame (called at 1011) runs frame.collect_schema().names() UNCONDITIONALLY whenever the node has a concrete required-column set (line 1520-1522), and _apply_selected_columns (1009) / _apply_column_renames (1010) each run an additional frame.collect_schema() when the node config carries selected_columns/column_renames. Because the per-node builder fn and its config are fixed and only the row DATA varies between chunks (the source file schema is constant), the resolved schema is byte-identical on chunk 0 and chunk N. The work is therefore recomputed C times where C = number of source batches. On the projection-driven chunk path required_columns_by_node is ALWAYS populated (chunk_plan line 784-824 sets it from projection.needed_by_node for both the explicit-chunk_size and byte-budget policies), so the _project_frame collect_schema fires for every chunk node on every chunk regardless of sizing policy. collect_schema() resolves the LazyFrame logical plan (every with_columns/cast/select in the chunk suffix) each call; it is not a free metadata read.
findings.evidence: Cost = O(N_chunk_nodes x N_chunks) logical-plan schema resolutions, each walking that node's accumulated lazy subplan, for a result that is constant across chunks. A 50M-row source at source_chunk_size 500k yields 100 chunks; a 6-node chunk suffix where 2 nodes also carry selected_columns/renames => ~ (6 + 2) x 100 = ~800 collect_schema() resolutions, ~99% of them recomputing an identical schema. The only correctness use of the result is (a) the missing-column guard in _project_frame (1524-1533) and (b) the projection column ordering (1534) - both invariant across chunks. No memoization exists: _project_frame (1514) and the two apply helpers take a fresh frame each call and cache nothing.
findings.when_it_bites: Any chunked execution over a large source: the streaming frontier auto-range job (routes/_optimiser_service.py:3757-3770 iterates iter_chunked_frames over the full scenario-expanded dataset) on multi-million-row ratebooks with deep chunk suffixes. Scales linearly with (chunk count x suffix depth); negligible for a handful of chunks, material at hundreds-to-thousands of chunks. The deeper the row-local polars/banding/rating chain, the more expensive each redundant collect_schema().
findings.recommended_fix: Resolve each chunk node's output column ordering and run the missing-column contract check ONCE (e.g. on the first non-empty chunk, or precompute from the projection plan's known per-node output columns) and reuse the cached ordered projection list for subsequent chunks. Equivalently, hoist the selected_columns/column_renames/projection resolution into a per-node closure built before the loop (alongside _build_funcs at 920-931) so the loop body only applies a precomputed select. Keep a one-time schema validation to preserve the fail-loud contract; drop the per-chunk re-resolution.

findings.location: src/haute/chunking.py:716 (chunk_plan prepare_graph) + 784 (plan_execution_strategy -> projection.plan -> prepare_graph at projection.py:2491) + 869 (iter_chunked_frames prepare_graph)
findings.title: prepare_graph runs three times per chunked execution (twice in chunk_plan, once in the runner) on identical inputs
findings.description: chunk_plan calls prepare_graph(request.graph, request.target_node_id, source=request.source) directly at line 716, then calls plan_execution_strategy at 784 which routes to projection.plan (projection.py:2489-2505) and calls prepare_graph again with the SAME (graph, target_node_id, source) arguments. iter_chunked_frames then calls prepare_graph a third time at line 869 (after _resolve_graph_paths). prepare_graph (projection.py:2109-2135) is O(V+E): ancestors() reverse-reachability, topo_sort_ids(), build_parents_of(), plus a _sanitize_func_name(label) per node. The three computations produce equivalent order/parents/id_to_name structures (the runner re-prepares on the canonicalised graph, but the topology is the same as planning). The plan already carries node_ids, pre_chunk_node_ids, chunk_node_ids, required_columns_by_node and edge_demands, so the runner's re-derivation of order/parents largely duplicates information the plan already proved.
findings.evidence: Three full graph preparations (two within a single chunk_plan call, one per iter_chunked_frames call) for one logical execution. Each is a topo sort + ancestor walk + per-node name sanitisation over the prepared subgraph. The duplication inside chunk_plan (716 vs 784) is pure waste - same args, same result - and is invisible to callers. The runner's prepare at 869 is partly justified (it operates on the path-resolved graph and must re-establish node_map/parents for execution) but still recomputes order/id_to_name that the plan could have carried.
findings.when_it_bites: Deep/wide graphs (hundreds of nodes, dense edges) and/or frequent planning. The optimiser auto-range planner builds a chunk_plan during job setup (_optimiser_service.py:922) and the runner re-prepares at job start (3757); a solve that re-plans per constraint sweep multiplies the O(V+E) prep. Setup-time only (not per chunk), so impact is bounded - real on large graphs, immaterial on small ones.
findings.recommended_fix: Inside chunk_plan, prepare the graph once and pass the prepared order/parents/node_map into the projection step via the already-existing prepared entry points (e.g. compute_prepared_plan / plan_prepared_execution_strategy at execution.py:213) instead of calling the graph-re-preparing plan_execution_strategy. For the runner, consider trusting the plan's node_ids/parents (already validated by _assert_plan_matches_prepared_graph and _assert_runner_shape) and only re-resolve what genuinely changes after _resolve_graph_paths, avoiding a third full topo sort.

findings.location: src/haute/chunking.py:1514-1535 (_project_frame allocations per node per chunk)
findings.title: _project_frame allocates two sets + a filtered list per node per chunk for an invariant projection ordering
findings.description: Independently of the collect_schema cost (finding 1), _project_frame rebuilds schema_set = set(schema_cols) (1523), missing = set(columns) - schema_set (1524), and ordered = [c for c in schema_cols if c in columns] (1534) on every node on every chunk. Since columns and the node's output schema are constant across chunks, both the membership-diff and the ordered projection list are identical each time. This is short-lived allocation churn layered on top of the redundant schema resolution.
findings.evidence: Two set constructions + one list comprehension per chunk node per chunk, all producing chunk-invariant results. At ~800 node-chunk iterations (the 100-chunk/8-node example) this is ~1600 transient sets + 800 lists with no caching, plus GC pressure - small per item but pure waste that vanishes once the projection ordering is memoised.
findings.when_it_bites: Same envelope as finding 1 (high chunk counts x suffix depth). On its own this is minor and would be a premature micro-optimisation; it is worth fixing only as a side effect of caching the projection ordering for finding 1, not as a standalone change.
findings.recommended_fix: Fold into finding 1: when the per-node ordered projection list is computed once and cached, these set/list allocations disappear automatically. Do not optimise in isolation.

results.coverage_note: Reviewed src/haute/chunking.py in full and traced its per-chunk dependencies (_execute_lazy._apply_selected_columns/_apply_column_renames/_build_funcs/_resolve_graph_paths, projection.prepare_graph/plan, execution.plan_execution_strategy, _polars_utils.streaming_collect/bounded_collect_batches/temporary_streaming_chunk_size) and both production call sites in routes/_optimiser_service.py (chunk_plan at 922, iter_chunked_frames at 3757). De-duplicated against review/02-findings (catalog.md, findings.json) and review/04-exhaustive (EXHAUSTIVE-FINDINGS.md, candidates.json): the already-known chunking items are the byte-budget downstream-column undercount (resource-leak), the dead _VARIABLE_WIDTH/_UNKNOWN_WIDTH constants, the validate_chunk_capability_declarations truthiness fallback, the unreachable _write_chunk_checkpoint unlink, and the local streaming_collect re-import; none overlap the three perf findings reported here. NOT reported because the code is already well-optimised at realistic scale: (a) the 128-row byte-sizing sample in _source_projected_column_widths (670-687) is a bounded one-time-per-plan cost (the architecture map's note 7 already flags only its UNDER-counting correctness, which is in 02-findings, not its runtime); (b) temporary_streaming_chunk_size is entered ONCE via the ExitStack at 938-941, not per chunk; (c) _build_funcs and the capability/AST-whitelist sweep (is_chunk_local_polars_code) run once per plan, not per chunk; (d) the per-chunk streaming_collect at 1029 and bounded_collect_batches at 952 are inherent to chunked execution. The single highest-impact item is the per-chunk collect_schema storm (finding 1); the prepare_graph triple-call (finding 2) and projection allocation churn (finding 3) are secondary. No files were modified.

findings.title: Rating-step applies N tables without threading input schema: collect_schema() re-resolved per table on a growing lazy plan (O(N^2))
findings.description: _apply_rating_step_outputs loops over tables (lf = _apply_rating_table(lf, table)) and never passes input_schema, so line 588 (frame_schema = input_schema if not None else _frame_schema(lf)) calls lf.collect_schema() every iteration. Each table appends ~5-7 lazy ops (key casts, left join, map_batches miss-guard, dtype reverts, rename/fill, drop), so the Nth collect_schema() walks a plan of size O(N); summed = O(N^2) plan traversal in Polars' schema resolver (no data read). The executor ratebook path (_builders.py:1644-1683) already fixed this: resolve schema ONCE into schema_by_name, thread via input_schema=schema_by_name, update incrementally (schema_by_name[out_col]=pl.Float64). deploy/_config.py:593 also threads input_schema. The shared rating-step path did not, so the asymmetry is an unintended miss, not a deliberate trade-off.
findings.evidence: sum_{k=1..N} O(k) = O(N^2) logical-plan node visits, pure overhead vs resolving the source schema once and tracking added Float64 columns. _combine_rating_output (line 772) adds one more collect_schema() per legacy combined output.
findings.when_it_bites: Insurance rating steps carry one factor table per factor (age, vehicle group, postcode, NCD, cover, occupation...); 10-50 tables is normal, complex ratebooks reach 100+. Paid per node execution: every preview, trace, batch row-group, AND every standalone pipeline.run() (apply_rating_step_from_config routes here -- the deploy/production path). Independent of row count: a 100-table step does ~100 schema resolutions over a plan up to ~700 nodes even on a 1-row quote.
findings.recommended_fix: Mirror the executor ratebook pattern: resolve the frame schema once in _apply_rating_step_outputs, pass it as input_schema to each _apply_rating_table call, and update a local schema map with each table's Float64 output (and combined-output) columns. _apply_rating_table already accepts input_schema. Factor columns are always pre-existing input columns, so a once-resolved schema stays correct for the revert-dtype/existing-column logic.

findings.title: JSON apiInput cache build fully materialises the file as Python objects with ~3-4x peak-memory copies, defeating the streaming iterator; bounded only by a wall-clock timeout
findings.description: build_per_port_cache does records = list(_iter_records(dp, ...)). _iter_records is a generator built to stream (used elsewhere with islice(sample_size)), but the build collapses it to a full in-memory list of dicts. shred_to_buffers makes a SECOND full copy (per-port lists of per-row dicts); _buffer_to_frame makes a THIRD per-column pass (values = [row.get(c) for row in rows]) before pl.Series. So the process simultaneously holds the decoded JSON object graph + per-port row-dict buffers + (transiently) per-column value lists, all boxed Python objects far larger than Arrow. No row/byte cap; only a coarse _BUILD_TIMEOUT in routes/json_cache.py. Arbitrary-nesting multi-port shred has no native Polars equivalent so some Python work is unavoidable, but holding three full copies and materialising the streaming JSONL iterator are avoidable.
findings.evidence: Peak RSS ~= all-records object graph + all per-port row dicts + one column value list, held at once, single-threaded. Python boxing ~3-10x on-disk bytes, so a few-hundred-MB JSONL can push multi-GB transient RSS. The list() at 825 discards the bounded-memory property the JSONL generator already provides (line-by-line at :342-353).
findings.when_it_bites: Clicking 'Cache as Parquet' on a large nested-JSON/JSONL apiInput dataset (hundreds of MB to low-GB). Single-process engine with no _ram_estimate admission on this path, so a large ingest can OOM the whole server where a chunked build stays bounded; only ceiling is the minutes-scale timeout. Small datasets unaffected.
findings.recommended_fix: For JSONL, shred in bounded record chunks: read a batch from _iter_records, shred_to_buffers on that batch, append each port's rows to a per-port pyarrow ParquetWriter (same pattern as _databricks_io.fetch_and_cache), release, repeat -- peak O(chunk) not O(file). At minimum drop list(...) so shred consumes the generator lazily, and build each Series from an iterator. Keep whole-file .json eager but gate it by a documented size threshold like the other bounded-memory profiles.

findings.title: Coverage note: Polars usage is otherwise well-optimised (no action)
findings.description: Reviewed in full: _polars_utils, _rating, _edge_join, _io, _json_flatten, _optimiser_apply_explainability, deploy/_impact; plus hot regions of _execute_lazy (eager core + lazy schema caching), projection, _json_shred, routes/_optimiser_service (auto-range + solve), _databricks_io, _model_scorer, modelling/_metrics, routes/_explore_service, deploy/_scorer, _builders, chunking. Cross-checked all 89 entries in review/02-findings/findings.json and the perf hot-paths map; the two findings above are NEW.
findings.evidence: collect_schema() is treated as data-free and cached in the executor (column_cache keyed by (node,port); schema_by_parent in join-key checks). Collects are streaming-first via streaming_collect with explicit allow_broad opt-in. Scans use projection/predicate pushdown (_io.read_source; _match_ratebook_input_row pushes equality filter into Polars and materialises only the matching row). Databricks ingest streams Arrow batches straight to parquet. Optimiser auto-range uses a bounded hash-partitioned external merge. Explore computes all per-column stats in ONE aggregation pass. Every iter_rows site operates on a bounded frame (preview row_limit, one quote's candidates, or head(top_n) after group_by). The rating miss-guard stays lazy/streaming via map_batches. No map_elements/apply-where-native-expr-exists and no to_pandas on a hot path found.
findings.when_it_bites: N/A -- informational.
findings.recommended_fix: No change required for the rest of the Polars surface.

findings.location: src/haute/_dataframe_execution_cache.py:235-301 (dataframe_execution_cache_key), 215-232 (_upstream_subgraph), 270-271; called per-node at src/haute/execution.py:653-666 and again at src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:806-845
findings.title: Per-node cache-key build rebuilds a full PipelineGraph and recomputes the base fingerprint from cold — O(N_target x (V+E)) graph reconstruction + hashing, done twice per run
findings.description: Every dataframe-execution cache key is derived by calling _upstream_subgraph(graph, node_id), which materialises a brand-new PipelineGraph via two full list comprehensions over graph.nodes and graph.edges (lines 220-232), then graph_fingerprint(lineage_graph). Because the lineage graph is a freshly constructed instance each time, its @cached_property _haute_base_fingerprint is always cold, so _graph_base_fingerprint runs in full: sorted(nodes by id) + canonical_json(config) per node + canonical_json([source,sourceHandle,target,targetHandle]) per edge + a sort of the serialized edge lines + an xxh64 over the joined parts. This entire pipeline runs once per node in the request-build loop (execution.py:653) and is then repeated verbatim in the _execute_lazy validation loop (_execute_lazy.py:829, 'expected_key = dataframe_execution_cache_key(...)') to assert the caller-supplied key matches. The GraphFingerprintMemo threaded through (execution.py:651, _execute_lazy.py:805) only memoises utility-file content hashes — it does NOT memoise the dominant base-fingerprint or subgraph work, so it provides no relief for the hot part.
findings.evidence: For a run materialising M cache nodes on a graph of V nodes / E edges, total cost is roughly 2 * sum_over_M( O(V) subgraph node filter + O(E) subgraph edge filter + O(V log V) node sort + O(V) canonical_json(config) + O(E) canonical_json(edge) + O(E log E) edge-line sort ). With M proportional to V this is O(V^2 + V*E) of pure-Python serialization+hashing per execution, paid twice (build + validate). canonical_json itself is a double pass: _canonicalise recursively rebuilds the structure, then _canonical_dumps calls json.dumps with sort_keys=True (a second key-sort of every mapping).
findings.when_it_bites: Large ratebooks / deep pipelines: a 200-node graph with several hundred edges where the lazy backend caches per-node outputs. The cost is paid on every lazy execution (every trace, every cached batch run, every preview that routes through the dataframe-exec cache) regardless of cache hit/miss, because key construction precedes the cache lookup. At 100+ nodes this is the hundreds-of-microseconds-per-node figure noted in _types.py:714 multiplied by node count and by 2, i.e. tens of milliseconds of CPU before any data is touched, growing quadratically with graph size.
findings.recommended_fix: Cache the per-(graph-instance, node_id) lineage fingerprint instead of rebuilding+rehashing. Two complementary options: (1) Compute each node's upstream-id set once for the whole graph (single reverse-topo pass) and reuse it across all target nodes rather than calling upstream_node_ids per node. (2) Memoise the lineage base fingerprint on GraphFingerprintMemo keyed by (id(graph), node_id) or by the frozenset of included node ids, so the request-build pass and the _execute_lazy validation pass share one computation instead of two. Even simpler for the validation pass: pass the already-built keys_by_node down and compare identity/fields without recomputing dataframe_execution_cache_key a second time. None of this changes digest bytes.

findings.title: upstream_node_ids uses a Python list as a FIFO with stack.pop(0) and stack[0:0]=... — both O(n) shifts, making the traversal O(V*E) on wide/deep lineages
findings.description: The BFS over parents uses stack.pop(0) (line 41) and stack[0:0] = parents_of.get(current, []) (line 45). list.pop(0) is O(len(stack)) because it shifts every remaining element left, and slice-assignment at index 0 (stack[0:0]=...) is O(len(stack)+len(inserted)) for the same reason. The frontier can hold O(V) ids for a wide graph, so the traversal degrades from the expected O(V+E) to O(V*E) in the worst case. This function is invoked inside _upstream_subgraph for every cache-key build (see finding above), so the slowdown compounds the per-node rebuild cost.
findings.evidence: Each of up to V dequeues costs O(frontier size); inserting parents at the head re-shifts the frontier. For a diamond/fan-in lineage with a wide parent layer the frontier is O(V) and the loop runs O(V) times => O(V^2) list shuffling per call, and this call itself is made per target node.
findings.when_it_bites: Deep or fan-in-heavy lineages (hundreds of upstream nodes feeding a target) on large ratebooks, multiplied by the number of cache nodes per run. Negligible on small graphs; clearly measurable once a single node's upstream set is in the hundreds and there are many such nodes.
findings.recommended_fix: Use collections.deque (popleft() is O(1)) and extend()/extendleft() instead of list.pop(0) and slice assignment. The result list is order-significant ('nearest parents first') but a deque preserves the same visitation order with O(1) ends. This is a drop-in change with no behavioural difference.

findings.title: Every cache get()/scan() re-validates the parquet artifact (filesystem exists() + scan_parquet().collect_schema()) under the global cache lock, on each hit
findings.description: Both get() (line 361) and scan() (line 370) open 'with self._lock:' and immediately call _evict_if_invalid(entry), which calls _validate_entry: entry.path.exists() (a stat syscall, line 543) followed by pl.scan_parquet(entry.path).collect_schema() (reads the parquet footer/metadata from disk, line 550) — all while still holding self._lock. The lock is the single mutex serialising every operation on the cache (get, scan, put, eviction, store-window bookkeeping, release_scan). So each cache lookup performs blocking filesystem + parquet-footer I/O inside the critical section, serialising all other threads' cache access behind disk latency, and re-reads the same footer on every hit even when the artifact has not changed since the last validation.
findings.evidence: _evict_if_invalid -> _validate_entry does 1 stat + 1 parquet metadata read per lookup; on a hot trace the same entry is scanned repeatedly (e.g. preview then trace reuse the same DataFrames) so the same footer is read each time. The work runs under self._lock (the with-block at lines 361 and 370 spans the _evict_if_invalid call), turning a pure in-memory LRU hit into a disk-bound, globally-serialised operation. materialize_lazy_frame_with_cache compounds this: on a miss it calls scan() twice (line 595 pre-store and line 615 post-store), so a single materialisation triggers two full validations.
findings.when_it_bites: Concurrent previews/traces against the same cache (multiple browser sessions or the trace layer reusing preview frames) on a busy server, especially on Windows/networked filesystems where parquet footer reads and stat() have higher latency. Also any workload with many small cache hits per second — each pays a parquet open under the global lock. Single-threaded local use barely notices.
findings.recommended_fix: Do not re-read the parquet footer on every hit. Validate lazily/cheaply: gate the expensive collect_schema() check behind a fast stat (size+mtime) comparison against the stored metadata, and skip re-validation entirely for an entry validated within the same operation. At minimum, drop self._lock before the collect_schema() I/O (hold it only to read/remove the entry record), so disk latency does not serialise unrelated cache operations. Keep the post-store validation (it guards a real corruption case) but avoid running it a second time in materialize_lazy_frame_with_cache when the entry was just written and validated.

findings.title: Eviction capacity check is O(n) per put and re-scans all entries on every loop iteration, with DataFrameExecutionCache adding a second full dict scan per candidacy test
findings.description: _evict_if_over_capacity (_lru_cache.py:295) recomputes _capacity_entry_count() — a full scan of self._data filtering by _is_pinned — on every iteration of the while loop and again after each eviction. DataFrameExecutionCache overrides _capacity_entry_count (line 517) to call super()._is_pinned per key, i.e. another O(n) scan, and its _is_pinned (line 515) consults _store_pins on top. So a single put that must evict k entries is O(k * n) capacity recomputation, and each candidate-selection inner loop (_lru_cache.py:302) re-materialises list(self._data.keys()) (O(n) allocation) per eviction.
findings.evidence: For default max_entries=16 the counts are tiny so this is invisible, but the structure is O(n) per put with an O(n) re-scan per evicted entry and a fresh O(n) key-list allocation per eviction step. The cost scales with cache size, not data size.
findings.when_it_bites: Only if max_entries is raised to a large value (hundreds+) AND the cache is churned heavily (many puts each forcing eviction), e.g. a long-lived server with a big dataframe-exec cache under constant invalidation. At the shipped default of 16 entries it does not matter.
findings.recommended_fix: Maintain a running unpinned-count and current_bytes incrementally (already tracked for bytes) rather than rescanning, and break the eviction victim search using the OrderedDict iteration order without re-listing all keys each pass. Low priority — note it only as a scalability ceiling on max_entries, not a present bottleneck.

findings.title: canonical_json double-sorts mapping keys: _canonicalise builds the dict then json.dumps(sort_keys=True) re-sorts every mapping
findings.description: _canonicalise already walks the whole value and produces canonical dicts/sorted sets; _canonical_dumps then calls json.dumps with sort_keys=True, which sorts the keys of every mapping a second time during serialization. The recursive _canonicalise pass also allocates a parallel copy of the entire structure (new lists for every list/tuple, new dict for every mapping) before serialization. For the fingerprint path this canonical_json runs once per node config and once per edge on every (cold) base-fingerprint computation.
findings.evidence: Two traversals + two sorts of each mapping per canonical_json call, plus a full structural copy. Combined with the per-node, twice-per-run base-fingerprint computation (finding 1), the constant factor is multiplied across V configs + E edges.
findings.when_it_bites: Large node configs (rating tables embedded as config, deep nested mappings) on big graphs, amplified by the per-node recompute in finding 1. On small configs it is in the noise.
findings.recommended_fix: Since _canonicalise already canonicalises ordering (sets sorted; mappings can be emitted in sorted-key order), drop sort_keys=True from _canonical_dumps and have _canonicalise emit mapping keys pre-sorted, eliminating the second sort. Verify byte-identical output against the existing fixtures (the canonicalisation contract is pinned by tests). Strictly an allocation/constant-factor win; do not pursue unless finding 1 is addressed and profiling still shows canonical_json hot.

findings.title: prepare_graph builds the reverse-adjacency (parents_of) twice per plan: once inside ancestors(), once directly
findings.description: prepare_graph() calls ancestors(target_node_id, edges, all_ids) (line 2121) to compute the target's ancestor set. ancestors() internally calls build_parents_of(edges, all_ids) over the FULL pruned edge list (every edge in the graph). prepare_graph() then immediately calls build_parents_of(relevant_edges, set(order)) AGAIN at line 2127 to build the parents_of it returns. Both are full linear scans over (almost) the same edge list, allocating a dict-of-lists keyed by every node. The first parents_of (built by ancestors) is discarded.
findings.evidence: ancestors() at _topo.py:107 does `parents = build_parents_of(edges, all_ids)` then BFS-walks it; the dict is thrown away on return (only `visited` survives). prepare_graph then does `parents_of = build_parents_of(relevant_edges, set(order))` at projection.py:2127. For a graph with E edges and N nodes both calls are O(E + N). When target_node_id is None, ancestors() is skipped (needed = all_ids), so this only bites the targeted-preview path — but that is the most frequent path (single-node preview, trace). The two scans differ only in edge filtering (full vs ancestor-filtered), so the first result is a strict superset and could be reused/filtered.
findings.when_it_bites: Every targeted preview/trace/single-node execution on a large graph. Concrete scale: a ratebook pipeline with ~500-2000 rating-step/banding nodes and a comparable edge count pays two full O(E+N) adjacency builds (plus a third in build_parents_of-via-children downstream) on each of the many previews an actuary triggers while iterating. At a few thousand edges the duplicate build is sub-millisecond per call, so this is a low-to-medium constant-factor win, not an algorithmic fix — worth folding in opportunistically, not a standalone hot fix.
findings.recommended_fix: Have ancestors() optionally return (or accept) the parents_of map it builds, or inline an ancestor walk in prepare_graph that reuses the single build_parents_of(relevant_edges,...) result by computing ancestors against the already-built reverse adjacency. One adjacency build per prepare_graph instead of two.

findings.title: plan() converts parents_of -> children_of, then compute_prepared_plan immediately rebuilds parents_by_child from children_of
findings.description: prepare_graph already produces parents_of (node -> parents). plan() throws it away and calls _children_of(order, parents_of) to invert it into children_of (line 2498, building a fresh dict-of-lists over all edges). compute_prepared_plan then re-inverts children_of back into parents_by_child (lines 2152-2156, another full dict-of-sets over all edges) because the reverse-topo sweep needs BOTH directions. So the planner does parents->children->parents, performing two extra full adjacency inversions when it already held parents_of upstream.
findings.evidence: plan(): `_children_of(prepared.order, prepared.parents_of)` (2498). _children_of iterates every (parent, child) pair to build children_of (2067-2070). compute_prepared_plan: `parents_by_child = {nid: set() ...}` then double loop over children_of re-adding every (parent,child) into parents_by_child (2152-2156). compute_prepared_plan's signature only accepts children_of, so the parents_of it could have reused is structurally inaccessible. Each inversion is O(E + N) and allocates N lists/sets.
findings.when_it_bites: Every plan() call (preview, trace, batch, deploy projection) on every graph. Two redundant O(E+N) inversions plus N set allocations. On a 2000-node ratebook with ~3000 edges this is a few-thousand-element rebuild done twice unnecessarily per plan; constant-factor, sub-ms at typical sizes. Matters mainly because plan() is on the per-preview path and the work is pure overhead — the data already exists.
findings.recommended_fix: Pass parents_of (or both maps) through to compute_prepared_plan instead of only children_of, and have it consume the existing parents_of directly rather than re-inverting children_of. children_of itself can be derived once if needed. Avoids one or both inversions.

findings.title: projection_contract(node) recomputed per node multiple times (own-node + once per child as 'parent_produced'), with no memoisation
findings.description: projection_contract(node) is the per-node contract resolver: it calls get_column_contract (registry lookup + contract callable), overlay_declared_contract (which may Contract.from_user_declared-parse the node's declared 'contract' config), and to_tuple(). compute_prepared_plan invokes it for the current node at line 2281. Separately, for any opaque-contract child it builds parent_produced = {pid: _parent_produced_columns(node_map[pid])} at lines 2283-2285, and _parent_produced_columns calls projection_contract(parent) AGAIN for each parent. Because every non-leaf node is a parent of >=1 child, a node's contract is frequently resolved 2+ times across the sweep (once as itself, once per opaque-contract child that lists it as a parent). The single-parent Polars rule (line 1286) adds yet another projection_contract(node) call for the SAME node before line 2281 is even reached.
findings.evidence: No @lru_cache / memo on projection_contract; it recomputes from node.data.config every call. Confirmed extra calls: (a) line 2281 `produced, referenced = projection_contract(node).to_tuple()`; (b) line 2284 `_parent_produced_columns(node_map[parent_id])` -> projection_contract(parent) for every parent, recomputed for that parent again when the parent is later visited as the current node; (c) SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule.parent_demands at 1286 calls projection_contract(node) and, when the node has a concrete contract, returns None at 1287 — so line 2281 then recomputes the identical contract. overlay_declared_contract re-parses node.data.config['contract'] via Contract.from_user_declared on each call when a contract annotation is present (declared_inputs_by_parent at 1789-1801 parses the same annotation a THIRD time for fan-in nodes).
findings.when_it_bites: Scales with (nodes that are parents of opaque-contract children) x (contract-resolution cost). Bites hardest on large ratebooks where many rating-step/banding nodes feed edge-join/optimiser/modelScore opaque nodes: each opaque child triggers a fresh contract build for ALL its parents, so a parent with K opaque children is resolved ~K+1 times. With user-declared 'contract' annotations the cost includes repeated Contract.from_user_declared validation/parsing of the same dict. At hundreds-to-thousands of nodes per plan, and plan() on every preview, this is the most defensible real redundant-recompute on the surface.
findings.recommended_fix: Memoise contract resolution per (node_id) for the duration of one compute_prepared_plan sweep — e.g. a local `contract_cache: dict[str, tuple[frozenset|None, frozenset|None]]` populated lazily and shared by the own-node path (2281), _parent_produced_columns (2284), the single-parent rule (1286), and declared_inputs_by_parent. Node contracts are pure functions of node.data.config and immutable within a plan, so caching is safe and removes the K-fold redo.

findings.title: User-code projection rules re-ast.parse and multi-walk the same code string several times per node
findings.description: For a single-parent Polars node, _single_parent_polars_expression_demands(code, ...) does ast.parse(code) once (line 1259), then runs _contains_rename_call (full ast.walk, 873-879), and if no rename, _contains_select_call (full ast.walk, 887-893) AND _references_derived_column (which internally does _derived_output_columns -> ast.walk 909, _referenced_polars_columns -> ast.walk 791, plus another ast.walk over select calls 947), then finally _unordered_expression_demands or _ordered_expression_demands (each another full ast.walk / iteration). That is 4-6 independent full traversals of the same AST per node. Separately, fan-in nodes call _join_calls_for_parent_inputs which does its OWN ast.parse(code) at line 1944 (a second parse of the same code), and join_parent_demands + PolarsFanInRule.parent_demands both call _join_calls_for_parent_inputs, re-parsing the code each time within a single node's processing.
findings.evidence: ast.parse appears at projection.py:1259, 1944 (and 512 for source code) — the 1944 parse re-parses code already parseable from the same node; _join_calls_for_parent_inputs is invoked from PolarsFanInRule.parent_demands at 1470 (joins) and again via join_parent_demands at 1482, and simple_join_calls_for_parent_inputs at 2018 — each call re-parses. _references_derived_column (927-958) alone triggers _derived_output_columns (ast.walk), _referenced_polars_columns (ast.walk), and a third select-scan ast.walk. ast.walk is a recursive generator over every node; running it 4-6x over one tree is pure constant-factor waste.
findings.when_it_bites: Bites per Polars feature-engineering / fan-in node WITH user code, proportional to code size. A typical pipeline has many such nodes; a node with a large with_columns/select body (dozens of expressions, common in pricing feature derivation) gets its AST walked 4-6 times and, for fan-in, parsed twice. On a ratebook/feature graph with hundreds of code-bearing Polars nodes evaluated on every plan(), the repeated walks dominate the planner's CPU. This is the clearest 'repeated graph walk' on the AST level called out in the focus.
findings.recommended_fix: Parse the node code once per node (cache the ast.Module on the node or in a per-sweep dict) and pass the tree into the rule helpers instead of re-parsing; combine the rename/select/derived-reference detection into a single ast.walk that collects all three signals in one pass; have PolarsFanInRule compute _join_calls_for_parent_inputs once and thread the result into join_parent_demands rather than letting each helper re-parse.

findings.title: strategy_summary_payload rebuilds a 5-way union node set and re-does diagnostics lookups per node on the preview-payload path
findings.description: strategy_summary_payload() materialises node_ids = sorted(set(needed_by_node) | set(materialisation_boundaries) | set(opaque_boundaries) | set(node_reasons) | set(opaque_reasons)) — five set() constructions plus a union plus a sort over every node (lines 159-165). It then loops every node calling _node_strategy(node_id), which itself does two dict .get() calls into diagnostics (133-135), and AGAIN fetches the same reason via diagnostics.node_reasons.get(node_id, diagnostics.opaque_reasons.get(...)) at 172-175 to populate the strategy dict — duplicating the lookup _node_strategy just performed. counts is accumulated for ALL nodes even though only max_nodes (100) strategies are retained.
findings.evidence: Lines 159-165 build/sort the full node-id set; 168-182 iterate it; _node_strategy (132-145) does diagnostics.node_reasons.get + opaque_reasons.get; lines 172-175 repeat the identical chained .get. For N nodes that is N x (2 + 2) dict lookups plus 5 full-set materialisations. The retained list is capped at 100 but the counts loop and the set unions are uncapped.
findings.when_it_bites: On the route/preview diagnostics path: strategy_summary_payload is called by diagnostics_payload to ship a compact summary to the UI. On a large ratebook (thousands of nodes) every preview that requests diagnostics re-materialises 5 full node-id sets and does ~4N dict lookups. It is bounded and not on the pure execution hot path, so low impact — but it is avoidable thrash when the same payload is requested repeatedly during interactive editing.
findings.recommended_fix: Build the node-id union once; in the loop compute the reason via a single .get and reuse it for both _node_strategy and the strategy dict (or have _node_strategy return (strategy, reason)). Optionally short-circuit the counts/strategies loop once both counts are stable and the retained cap is reached if exact per-strategy totals beyond the cap are not required.

findings.location: src/haute/projection.py:2152-2156 (compute_prepared_plan) vs 2245-2246 (parents_by_child.get) and rule entry points (e.g. 1283, 1318, 1441, 1578, 1942)
findings.title: parent_ids passed as a set then re-materialised with set(parent_ids)/list(parent_ids) inside nearly every rule
findings.description: compute_prepared_plan builds parents_by_child as dict[str, set[str]] (line 2152) and passes parent_ids = parents_by_child.get(node_id, set()) (line 2245) — already a set — into the rule pipeline. Almost every rule then defensively re-materialises it: OptimiserParentDemandRule `parent_set = set(parent_ids)` (662), OpaqueContractRule `set(parent_ids)` (1318), PolarsFanInRule `set(parent_ids)` (1441), EdgeJoinFanInRule `set(parent_ids)` (1578) plus sorted() of it (1580), SingleParentPolarsExpressionRule `list(parent_ids)` (1283), _join_calls_for_parent_inputs `set(parent_ids)` (1942), edge_join_fan_in_demands_for_node `set(parent_ids)` (1639) computed just to take len(). Because parent_demands_for_node tries the optimiser rule AND the single-parent rule, and the opaque/fan-in paths each re-set again, a single node can re-copy its parent set 3-5 times.
findings.evidence: Confirmed set()/list() re-materialisation sites: projection.py:662, 1283, 1318, 1441, 1578-1580, 1639, 1942. The input is already a set (2245). edge_join_fan_in_demands_for_node at 1639 does `len(set(parent_ids)) <= 1` purely to count, allocating a set to discard it. Each is O(P) for P parents and allocates a new container.
findings.when_it_bites: Per node, multiplied by the number of rule attempts. Negligible for the typical 1-3 parents per node, but on wide fan-in nodes (an edge-join or optimiser with many declared parents, or a big multi-source merge) the parent set is copied several times per node across rule attempts. Pure constant-factor; only worth tidying alongside the larger contract-memoisation change, not on its own.
findings.recommended_fix: Accept that parent_ids is already a set at the call site and pass it through (or normalise once to a frozenset in compute_prepared_plan and let rules consume it without re-copying). Replace `len(set(parent_ids)) <= 1` count-only checks with a length that does not allocate (e.g. operate on the already-set value).
